Name: Katie Eden
Badge: Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

I thoroughly enjoyed the process of the layered writing. Having students jot down notes on what stood out and their thinking allows them to reflect and see how their perspective changes or stays the same. Students felt like they had a clear stand on the argument and the writing flowed.

Think back to a moment during the lesson sequence that stands out. It could be a comment from a student, an unexpected challenge or success, a shift in engagement, or a moment when your own thinking changed. Describe what happened and why this moment feels meaningful to you now. What does it reveal:
Reading the article and having students jot down their thinking and then share allowed students to form their own perspective and then share with others. I feel like sometimes students "jump on the bandwagon" and just agree with their partner. However, allowing them to write it down and then share gave them ownership.
As you look over the drafts your students produced in this lesson sequence, what early patterns, surprises, or questions are emerging for you? We incorporated this with our MRI model for argumentative writing. Students felt prepared to write and reference the articles with ease. One thing that students talked about was that the articles leaned more towards one side of the argument and would have liked more of a variety. I enjoyed reading my students writings and was pleased with how they turned out.
